summary: Carolee Schneemann was an American feminist performance artist, best known for Interior Scroll, in which she read from a scroll pulled out of her vagina, and Meat Joy, in which performers in underwear rolled around in raw fish, chicken and sausages. Her film Fuses documents her having sex with her partner, the composer James Tenney, while her cat Kitch looks on. Her book Cezanne, She Was a Great Painter contains the text of Interior Scroll, and she was suspended from Bard College for painting a nude self-portrait.
comprehensive_summary:
Carolee Schneemann was an American feminist performance artist who worked mainly in New York City and is named with Allan Kaprow as a practitioner of performance art, and with Barbara Kruger and Judy Chicago as an American feminist artist. Early in her career she painted a nude self-portrait, which got her suspended from Bard College for "moral turpitude"; during the suspension she met the composer James Tenney. A text by Schneemann describes a "structuralist filmmaker" who told her "we can be friends equally tho we are not artists equally." In 1999 she answered Daniel Socolow's request to recommend someone else for a MacArthur "Genius Grant" with the indignant line "I do not have health insurance."

Her most famous performance, Interior Scroll, took place in New York City. She announced that she would read from her book Cezanne, She Was a Great Painter, and then pulled a long scroll out of her vagina and read the text aloud. In her essay "The Obscene Body/Politic" she wrote that she had not wanted to perform the primary action of this 1975 piece, but that the "culture's terror" of the act made it necessary. The book Cezanne, She Was a Great Painter grew out of a misunderstanding that led her to think the painter of Pyramid of Skulls, Paul Cezanne, was a woman; its cover shows a figure looking in a mirror, made when she was four years old.

Meat Joy is the orgy-like piece in which Schneemann and seven other performers, wearing underwear, dance, fall to the floor, and then sensually roll around in raw fish, chicken, sausages and livers spread on a plastic sheet. At its premiere a man jumped onstage and tried to strangle her. The silent film Fuses documents her having sex with James Tenney while her cat Kitch looks on; she made it after a bad experience acting in an erotic film by Stan Brakhage, and described it to Maggie Nelson as a "heterosexual classic."

Cats run through much of her work. In the photo series Infinity Kisses she photographed herself "deep kissing" her cats, often in out-of-focus Polaroids of a morning ritual. When one of her cats died she had its body taxidermied ahead of a performance of Up to and Including Her Limits, in which she drew on walls while strapped in a harness. The installation More Wrong Things includes photographs of a cat hit by a car, and the film Kitch's Last Meal features her 18th-century house in upstate New York. In the Eye Body series she brought "shamanic ritual" to the nude in photos inspired by Cretan snake goddesses, and she performed thirty-six "transformative actions" amid broken glass. She also posed as a live version of Edouard Manet's Olympia in Robert Morris's performance Site at the Judson Dance Theater. Other works include Mortal Coils, dedicated to fifteen friends including John Cage, an assemblage of four cutting boards with scraps of hair, and an unrealized piece about the bodies of Syrian refugees that she described to Pipilotti Rist.
